Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

visible adjective

also in sight, in view, can be seen, out of sight

classical

Caes. BG 1.11: paene in cōnspectū exercitūs nostrī (Lewis & Short)
Liv. 1.39.1: multōrum in cōnspectū

in cōnspectū esse

phrase: in + the ablative of cōnspectus; whose sight, in the genitive or a possessive

be in sight, be visible

Latin says where a thing can be seen rather than calling it visible: in cōnspectū est, it is in sight; out of sight is ē cōnspectū (Ter. Eun. 2.3.2, illam ē cōnspectū āmīsī meō, Lewis & Short). For “it can be seen” the verb does the work: cernitur, appāret (see appear).

Other words

  • cōnspicuus, cōnspicua, cōnspicuum — visible, in view; that catches the eye

    also used · classical · Ov. Tr. 4.10.108: occultum stēllae cōnspicuumque polum (Lewis & Short); Tac. Germ. 7.1 · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx poētica et aetātis post-Augustēae: Ov., Hor., Tac.)

    First “in view”, opposed to occultus; more often “striking, conspicuous”, standing out from the rest (Liv. 1.34.11). Lewis & Short: poetic, or post-Augustan prose, especially Tacitus; not in Quintilian.

  • aspectābilis, aspectābile — visible

    also used · classical · Cic. Tim. 4 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Cicero’s word in his version of Plato’s Timaeus, for the visible world; Lewis & Short knows it perhaps only there. A philosopher’s word.

  • vīsibilis, vīsibile — visible

    also used · late Latin · Apul. Mund.; Prud. Apoth. 146 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    Late Latin for Cicero’s aspectābilis (Lewis & Short); in the one classical passage, Plin. NH 11.146, it means “able to see”.

Examples

  • puerō dormientī, cui Serviō Tulliō fuit nōmen, caput ārsisse ferunt multōrum in cōnspectū

    they say that as a boy called Servius Tullius lay asleep, his head blazed with fire in full view of many peopleLiv. 1.39.1

  • ducēs exemplō potius quam imperiō, sī prōmptī, sī cōnspicuī, sī ante aciem agant, admīrātiōne praesunt

    the chiefs lead by example rather than by command: if they are ready, if they are in plain view, if they fight in front of the line, they lead by being admiredTac. Germ. 7.1

  • Ecce, jam lūna in cōnspectū est!

    Look, you can see the moon now!composed

See also appear, see.
